Traditional Christmas Pudding

Served at: Christmas Day

Serves 8-10Prep 45 minCook Initial steaming: 8 hours; Reheating: 2 hours

Christmas Pudding is a rich, steamed dessert that has been a festive centerpiece of British Christmas dinners for centuries. Often prepared weeks or even months in advance, it symbolizes the bounty and warmth of the holiday season, traditionally brought to the table flaming with brandy.

Ingredients

  • 1 cup (150g) raisins
  • 1 cup (150g) currants
  • 1 cup (150g) sultanas (golden raisins)
  • 1/2 cup (75g) candied mixed peel, finely chopped
  • 1/2 cup (75g) glacé cherries, halved
  • 1/2 cup (120ml) dark stout or ale (like Guinness)
  • 1/4 cup (60ml) brandy or dark rum, plus extra for flaming
  • 1 cup (120g) fresh breadcrumbs
  • 1 cup (120g) self-rising flour
  • 1 cup (200g) dark brown sugar, packed
  • 1 cup (120g) shredded beef suet
  • 1 teaspoon mixed spice
  • 1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon
  • 1/4 teaspoon freshly grated nutmeg
  • Zest of 1 orange
  • Zest of 1 lemon
  • 2 large eggs, beaten
  • 1 small apple, peeled, cored, and grated (e.g., Bramley or Granny Smith)

Method

  1. In a large bowl, combine the raisins, currants, sultanas, candied peel, and glacé cherries. Pour the stout/ale and 1/4 cup (60ml) brandy/rum over the fruit, stir well, cover, and let it soak overnight or for at least 12 hours.
  2. The next day, generously grease a 2-quart (2-liter) pudding basin with butter. Cut a circle of parchment paper to fit the bottom of the basin and place it inside.
  3. In a very large mixing bowl, combine the soaked fruit mixture with the breadcrumbs, self-rising flour, dark brown sugar, shredded suet, mixed spice, ground cinnamon, grated nutmeg, orange zest, lemon zest, beaten eggs, and grated apple.
  4. Stir all the ingredients thoroughly until well combined. Traditionally, every family member takes a turn stirring the pudding mixture and making a wish.
  5. Spoon the mixture into the prepared pudding basin, pressing it down lightly. Do not fill to the very top; leave about 1 inch (2.5 cm) of space for expansion.
  6. Cover the top of the pudding basin with a double layer of parchment paper and then a layer of aluminum foil, securing it tightly with kitchen twine around the rim. Create a handle with the twine for easy lifting.
  7. Place the pudding basin in a large pot with a tight-fitting lid. Pour boiling water into the pot until it comes halfway up the sides of the pudding basin.
  8. Bring the water to a simmer, then cover the pot and steam the pudding for 8 hours, checking the water level periodically and topping up with boiling water as needed to prevent it from boiling dry.
  9. After 8 hours, carefully remove the pudding from the pot and let it cool completely. Once cool, remove the foil and parchment paper, then replace with fresh layers of parchment and foil. Store in a cool, dark place for at least 2-3 weeks, or up to 3 months, to allow the flavors to mature. You can 'feed' it periodically with a tablespoon of brandy or rum by poking holes in the top.
  10. On Christmas Day, re-steam the pudding for 2 hours using the same method as before.
  11. To serve, carefully invert the hot pudding onto a serving plate. For a dramatic presentation, warm a small amount of extra brandy in a ladle over a flame (or carefully in a saucepan), ignite it, and pour it over the pudding just before serving.
  12. Serve immediately with brandy butter, custard, or cream.

Tips

  • For the best flavor, make your Christmas pudding at least 2-3 weeks in advance, or even up to three months, allowing the flavors to deepen and mature.
  • To 'feed' the pudding, poke a few holes in the top after it has cooled and drizzle a tablespoon of brandy or rum over it once a week until Christmas.
  • Ensure the water level in the steaming pot is always maintained; if it boils dry, the pudding can scorch.
